tiles.title: The Spreadsheet Grid and Cell References
tiles.summary: Introduces the spreadsheet grid model (cells, rows, columns, sheets) and A1 cell references and ranges, using the QuickDeliver orders workbook as context.

steps.title: Every cell has an address
steps.lede: A spreadsheet is a grid of cells, each one named by its column letter and row number.

blocks.text: Open a new workbook and you already have structure before you type anything. Cells are grouped into rows and columns, forming a grid, and each cell can hold a number, text, or a formula. Think of it like a table where every slot has its own name.

Each cell's name is its address: the column letter followed by the row number. Excel uses the A1 reference style by default — columns are letters, rows are numbers. So the cell at the intersection of column B and row 2 is called B2. If you type a delivery city into the second row of the second column, you're typing into B2.

blocks.alt_text: A small spreadsheet grid showing column letters A, B, C across the top and row numbers 1, 2, 3 down the side. Cell B2 is highlighted with a callout showing its address. Two sheet tabs at the bottom are labelled Sheet1 and Sheet2.

steps.title: One workbook, many sheets
steps.lede: A workbook can hold multiple sheets, each with its own grid.

blocks.text: A workbook is not limited to one grid. It can contain multiple sheets — you can add as many as you need. By default Excel names them Sheet1, Sheet2, Sheet3 and so on; the name appears on the sheet tab at the bottom and can be renamed. A QuickDeliver workbook might start with Sheet1 for orders and Sheet2 for drivers, then you rename each tab to Orders and Drivers.

steps.title: Pointing at one cell or many
steps.lede: A reference tells Excel exactly which cell or cells to use in a formula.

blocks.text: A reference identifies a cell or a range of cells on a worksheet and tells Excel where to look for the values a formula needs. Without a reference, a formula can only work with numbers you type directly — references let it reach into the grid.

In the A1 reference style, a single cell is referred to by its column letter followed by its row number — for example B2. That is the same address you would use to describe one order's city in the Orders sheet.

A reference can also point at a block of cells at once. A10:A20 refers to the range in column A, rows 10 through 20. A10:E20 refers to the range in columns A through E, rows 10 through 20. If delivery times sit in column C, rows 2 through 21, then C2:C21 covers every delivery time in that batch.

annotations.text: Rectangular range A10:E20 — rows 10 through 20, columns A through E

steps.title: Referencing an entire row or column
steps.lede: Use a repeated letter or number to select every cell in a column or row.

blocks.text: You can reference an entire row or column by repeating its letter or number on either side of a colon: 5:5 selects all cells in row 5, and H:H selects all cells in column H. If new orders keep being added to the Orders sheet and you want a reference that always covers the whole city column, B:B does that.

steps.title: The grid, addresses, and ranges
steps.lede: Everything in a spreadsheet starts from the cell address and the range.

blocks.text: A cell is found by its column-letter/row-number address, and a workbook can hold several grids as separate sheets. A reference points at one cell or a block of cells; a range like A10:E20 covers a rectangular block, while H:H covers an entire column. Every formula you write from here will use one of these reference forms.

remediation_steps.title: Re-check: address vs. contents
remediation_steps.lede: A cell's address and its contents are two different things — here is the contrast.

blocks.text: The address B2 is the cell's location — column B, row 2. The contents of B2 is whatever you have typed or calculated there: a number, a city name, or a formula. Changing the contents does not change the address; B2 is always B2 regardless of what is inside it.

remediation_steps.title: Re-check: grid structure and sheet names
remediation_steps.lede: Rows, columns, and sheet tabs — a quick contrast to clear up confusion.

blocks.text: Columns run left to right and are labelled with letters (A, B, C…). Rows run top to bottom and are labelled with numbers (1, 2, 3…). A workbook can hold multiple sheets; by default they are named Sheet1, Sheet2 and so on, and each name appears on its tab at the bottom of the screen.

remediation_steps.title: Re-check: whole-row and whole-column notation
remediation_steps.lede: The colon syntax for selecting an entire row or column — a clear contrast.

blocks.text: To reference all cells in row 5, write 5:5 — the row number on both sides of the colon. To reference all cells in column H, write H:H — the column letter on both sides. This is different from a rectangular range like A10:E20, which uses different start and end addresses. H:H always expands as new rows are added.

remediation_steps.title: Re-check: single-cell and range references
remediation_steps.lede: Single cells, rectangular blocks, and whole-column references — the three forms side by side.

blocks.text: A single-cell reference uses column letter then row number: B2. A rectangular range uses a start address, a colon, and an end address: A10:E20 covers columns A through E, rows 10 through 20. A whole-column reference repeats the letter: B:B covers every cell in column B. A formula picks the form that matches how many cells it needs.

steps.title: Every Formula Starts with =

blocks.text: In your QuickDeliver Orders sheet, most cells hold plain values — an amount, a city, a date. A formula changes that: it tells Excel to compute a result instead. Every formula begins with the equal sign (=). Without it, Excel treats the entry as text.

Excel's four arithmetic operators are + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), and / (division). You can combine them with literal numbers or cell addresses: =D3-D2 subtracts one order's amount from another; =D2*2 doubles it. To reference another cell, type its address after the = and operator.

Built-in functions follow the same = prefix but add a name and parentheses: =SUM(D2:D21) totals every amount in that range of your Orders sheet. Type =, the function name, an opening parenthesis, select the range, close the parenthesis, then press Enter. The cell shows the computed result.

steps.lede: A formula turns a cell into a calculator — here's the pattern every formula follows.

steps.title: Operator Precedence and Parentheses

blocks.text: Excel evaluates multiplication and division before addition and subtraction. =5+2*3 gives 11, not 21. Wrap the addition in parentheses — =(5+2)*3 — to get 21. Whenever a formula mixes operators, check the order or add parentheses to be explicit.

steps.lede: Multiplication runs before addition — unless you use parentheses.

steps.title: Relative and Absolute References

blocks.text: A relative reference such as D2 is position-based: copy the formula one row down and D2 becomes D3 automatically. By default, every new formula uses relative references. This is what you want when each row should calculate against its own data.

An absolute reference such as $H$1 always points to the same cell, no matter where you copy the formula. Dollar signs lock both the column letter and the row number. If a delivery fee rate lives in H1, =D2*$H$1 copied down every order row keeps pointing to H1 for the rate while D2 shifts to D3, D4, and so on.

blocks.change_summary: After copying H2 down to H3 and H4, the relative part (D2→D3→D4) adjusts while the absolute part ($H$1) stays fixed.

steps.lede: Copy a formula down a column and watch which parts shift — and which stay fixed.

steps.title: Mixed References: Lock One Dimension

blocks.text: A mixed reference locks only one dimension. $A1 locks the column (A stays, row shifts); A$1 locks the row (1 stays, column shifts). Use a mixed reference when copying a formula across both rows and columns and only one axis should stay fixed.

steps.lede: Lock just the column or just the row — not both.

steps.title: Formulas and Reference Types — Key Takeaways

blocks.text: Every formula starts with =, combines cell references and operators or a function call, and follows Excel's precedence rules unless parentheses override them. Relative references shift when copied; absolute references ($A$1) stay fixed; mixed references lock one dimension. That combination is the basis for every calculation you'll write in a spreadsheet.

blocks.title: Up Next: Aggregation Functions
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll use SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, and COUNTA to summarise the entire Orders column in a single formula.

Excel distinguishes a formula from plain text by the leading = sign. Type 5+2 and Excel stores the text '5+2'. Type =5+2 and Excel computes 7. Every formula — whether it uses arithmetic operators or a function like SUM — must start with =.

A function formula follows the pattern =NAME(range). =SUM(D2:D21) is correct: equal sign, function name, opening parenthesis, the range, closing parenthesis. Omitting the = or the parentheses produces an error or plain text, not a computed result.

A mixed reference uses exactly one $ sign. $A1 locks the column letter A — copy the formula across columns and A never changes, but the row number shifts. A$1 locks the row number 1 — copy down rows and 1 never changes, but the column shifts. Two $ signs ($A$1) lock both and make the reference fully absolute.

steps.title: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, and COUNTA

blocks.text: With a full column of delivery amounts or times, you often want one summary number. SUM adds every value in a range: =SUM(D2:D21) totals all order amounts on your Orders sheet. AVERAGE returns the arithmetic mean: =AVERAGE(C2:C21) gives the average delivery time, skipping blank cells and text but including any cell that contains zero (Pending or Cancelled orders with no recorded time are blank, not zero, so they are excluded).

blocks.takeaway: COUNT returns a smaller number than COUNTA when the column contains blanks or text, because COUNT skips non-numeric cells while COUNTA counts everything that is not empty.

steps.lede: Four functions that reduce a whole column to one summary number.

steps.title: COUNT vs COUNTA: What Gets Counted

blocks.text: COUNT counts only cells that contain numbers; empty cells, text, and error values are skipped. On your Orders sheet, =COUNT(C2:C21) counts only the rows where delivery_minutes is recorded (Delivered orders) — Pending and Cancelled rows with NULL times are excluded.

COUNTA counts every cell that is not empty, regardless of type — numbers, text, or error values all count. =COUNTA(C2:C21) on the same column returns a larger number than COUNT because it includes any row that has any value at all. Use COUNTA when you need to count rows, not just numeric entries.

steps.lede: The difference matters whenever a column mixes numbers, blanks, or text.

steps.title: IF, Nested IF, AND, and OR

blocks.text: IF tests a condition and returns one value when it is TRUE and another when it is FALSE. Its syntax is IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false). Text results go in quotes: =IF(C2>60,"Late","On Time") placed in a helper column (H) labels each order row based on its delivery_minutes value without overwriting the amount column.

Multiple IF functions can be nested to handle more than two outcomes. =IF(H2>89,"A",IF(H2>79,"B",IF(H2>69,"C",IF(H2>59,"D","F")))) converts a numeric score to a letter grade. The same structure could sort orders into delivery-time bands in a helper column instead of a single Late/On-Time split.

steps.lede: Label, flag, or categorise rows based on conditions — without changing the data.

steps.title: AND and OR: Testing Multiple Conditions

blocks.text: AND returns TRUE only when all of its arguments are TRUE; if any one is FALSE, AND returns FALSE. Its syntax is AND(logical1, logical2, ...). Use AND as the logical_test of IF to require every condition to hold: =IF(AND(C2>30,E2="Delivered"),"Fast Delivery","Other") flags only orders that are both fast and delivered.

OR returns TRUE when any of its arguments is TRUE; it returns FALSE only when all arguments are FALSE. Its syntax is OR(logical1, logical2, ...). =IF(OR(E2="Pending",E2="Cancelled"),"Not Delivered","Delivered") flags any order that has not yet completed.

steps.lede: Combine conditions inside IF to test more than one thing at once.

steps.title: Aggregation and Logical Functions — Key Takeaways
steps.lede: What you've learned in this tile.

blocks.text: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, and COUNTA each reduce a range to one number; which one you reach for depends on whether you need a total, a mean, a count of numbers, or a count of anything non-blank. IF tests a condition and returns different values for TRUE and FALSE; nest IFs for multiple outcomes, and use AND or OR to combine conditions.

blocks.title: Up Next: Text, Date, and Conditional Aggregation
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll combine and extract text with TEXTJOIN and LEFT/RIGHT/MID, calculate date differences with TODAY and DATEDIF, and count or sum only the rows that meet a condition with COUNTIF and SUMIFS.

remediation_steps.title: Matching the Function to the Task

blocks.text: SUM totals numbers. AVERAGE finds the mean (blank cells are skipped, zero-value cells are included). COUNT counts only numeric cells — blank and text cells are excluded. COUNTA counts every non-blank cell regardless of type. On the Orders sheet: use SUM for total amount, AVERAGE for mean delivery time, COUNT for how many deliveries have a recorded time, COUNTA for how many rows have any entry.

IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false) evaluates the test first. If the test is TRUE, the formula returns value_if_true; if FALSE, value_if_false. =IF(C2>60,"Late","On Time"): when C2 is 45, the test 45>60 is FALSE, so the formula returns "On Time". Text values in IF must be wrapped in quotes.

remediation_steps.title: AND Requires All; OR Requires Any

blocks.text: AND(condition1, condition2) returns TRUE only when every condition is TRUE — one FALSE makes the whole AND FALSE. OR(condition1, condition2) returns TRUE when at least one condition is TRUE — it returns FALSE only when every condition is FALSE. Use AND when all criteria must hold; use OR when any one is enough.

steps.title: Combining Text with TEXTJOIN and CONCATENATE

blocks.text: TEXTJOIN combines text from multiple ranges or strings and inserts a delimiter between each value. Its syntax is TEXTJOIN(delimiter, ignore_empty, text1, text2, ...). Setting ignore_empty to TRUE skips blank cells rather than joining them as empty strings. On your Orders sheet, TEXTJOIN(", ", TRUE, B2, E2) would merge the city and status columns, skipping any blank status.

CONCATENATE joins two or more text strings into one: CONCATENATE(text1, text2, ...). Microsoft recommends using the newer CONCAT function instead, as CONCATENATE may not be available in future versions of Excel. CONCATENATE does not add a separator automatically — include it as a literal argument. TEXTJOIN uses its delimiter argument to insert one for you.

steps.lede: Merge values from separate cells into one string — with or without a separator.

steps.title: Extracting Text with LEFT, RIGHT, MID, and TRIM

blocks.text: LEFT returns the first N characters of a string: LEFT(text, num_chars). RIGHT returns the last N characters: RIGHT(text, num_chars). On order IDs like "LG-2001", =LEFT(A2,2) returns "LG" and =RIGHT(A2,4) returns "2001".

MID returns characters from any position: MID(text, start_num, num_chars). =MID(A2,4,4) on "LG-2001" starts at position 4 and takes 4 characters, returning "2001". TRIM removes all extra spaces — leading, trailing, and multiple spaces between words — leaving only single spaces between words: TRIM(text). If a city was imported as " Lagos ", =TRIM(B2) returns "Lagos".

blocks.change_summary: LEFT extracts the two-character prefix from the order ID; TRIM removes the stray spaces from the city name.

steps.lede: Pull specific characters out of a string — or strip unwanted spaces.

steps.title: TODAY, DATEDIF, and the Date Serial Number

blocks.text: Excel stores every date as a sequential serial number: January 1, 1900 is 1, and each subsequent day adds 1. That is why date functions can do arithmetic on dates the same way ordinary functions do on numbers — a date cell is just a number displayed in a date format.

TODAY() returns the serial number of the current date and takes no arguments. DATEDIF(start_date, end_date, unit) returns the difference between two dates in the unit you specify: "Y" for complete years, "D" for days. DATEDIF is useful for age calculations: DATEDIF(birthdate, TODAY(), "Y") returns the number of complete years between the birthdate and today.

On your Orders sheet, with an order date in G2, =DATEDIF(G2,TODAY(),"D") tells you how many days have passed since that order was placed. TODAY() supplies the end date automatically, so the result updates each day the workbook is opened.

steps.lede: Excel stores dates as numbers — which makes date arithmetic straightforward.

steps.title: COUNTIF and SUMIF: One Condition

blocks.text: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, and COUNTA take every value in their range. When you only want rows that meet a condition — orders from Lagos, say — use COUNTIF or SUMIF instead.

COUNTIF(range, criteria) counts the cells in range that match criteria. =COUNTIF(B2:B21,"Lagos") counts how many orders in the city column are from Lagos. SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range) sums the values in sum_range for rows where range matches criteria. =SUMIF(B2:B21,"Lagos",D2:D21) totals the amounts for Lagos orders only.

annotations.text: SUMIF — criteria range + criterion + sum range

steps.lede: Count or sum only the rows that match a single criterion.

steps.title: COUNTIFS and SUMIFS: Multiple Conditions

blocks.text: COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, criteria_range2, criteria2, ...) counts rows where all criteria are met together. Each additional range must have the same number of rows and columns as the first. =COUNTIFS(B2:B21,"Lagos",E2:E21,"Delivered") counts only Lagos orders that are Delivered.

SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, criteria_range2, criteria2, ...) sums sum_range for rows where all criteria hold. Note the argument order: sum_range comes first, then each criteria_range/criteria pair. =SUMIFS(D2:D21,B2:B21,"Lagos",E2:E21,"Delivered") totals amounts for Lagos Delivered orders.

steps.lede: Add a second (or third) condition by extending the argument list.

steps.title: Criteria Syntax and the Between Pattern

blocks.text: Criteria can be a number, an expression, a cell reference, or text. Criteria that contain comparison symbols or text must be enclosed in quotation marks: use ">32" not >32, and "Lagos" not Lagos. A bare number like 32 or a cell reference like B4 does not need quotes.

The same range can appear in more than one criteria pair to test a between condition. =COUNTIFS(C2:C21,">30",C2:C21,"<60") counts orders where delivery_minutes is between 30 and 60 — both criteria apply to the same column.

steps.lede: Criteria with comparison symbols or text must be in quotes — and you can use the same range twice.

steps.title: Text, Date, and Conditional Aggregation — Key Takeaways

blocks.text: TEXTJOIN combines text with a delimiter; CONCATENATE (or CONCAT) joins without one. LEFT, RIGHT, and MID extract characters by position; TRIM removes stray spaces. Excel stores dates as serial numbers starting from January 1, 1900; TODAY() returns today's serial number and DATEDIF computes the difference in years or days. COUNTIF and SUMIF apply one condition; COUNTIFS and SUMIFS apply multiple — criteria with text or comparison symbols must be in quotes.

blocks.title: Up Next: VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP, and INDEX/MATCH
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll look up a driver name from the Drivers sheet using VLOOKUP, then see how XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH handle cases VLOOKUP cannot.

TEXTJOIN(delimiter, ignore_empty, text1, text2, ...) has three required parts. The delimiter is the separator inserted between each value. ignore_empty controls blank cells: TRUE skips them so no extra delimiter appears; FALSE includes them as empty strings. TEXTJOIN(", ", TRUE, B2, E2) on a row where E2 is blank returns just the city, not "Lagos, ".

MID(text, start_num, num_chars) needs three arguments: the text, where to start (1-based), and how many characters to take. =MID(A2,4,4) on "LG-2001" starts at position 4 (the '2') and takes 4 characters, returning "2001". TRIM(text) takes one argument and removes all leading and trailing spaces, leaving only single spaces between words.

TODAY() returns the current date as a serial number and takes no arguments — it is always =TODAY() with empty parentheses. DATEDIF(start_date, end_date, unit) computes the difference between two dates. Use "D" as the unit for days and "Y" for complete years. To find days since an order was placed: =DATEDIF(G2,TODAY(),"D").

COUNTIF and SUMIF each accept exactly one criteria range and one criterion. COUNTIFS and SUMIFS accept any number of criteria_range/criteria pairs — all conditions must be met for a row to be counted or summed. For two conditions (city = Lagos AND status = Delivered), use COUNTIFS or SUMIFS, not COUNTIF or SUMIF.

remediation_steps.title: Using the Same Range Twice for a Between Condition

blocks.text: COUNTIFS allows the same range to appear in more than one criteria pair. To count values between 30 and 60 in C2:C21, write: =COUNTIFS(C2:C21,">30",C2:C21,"<60"). The first pair filters rows where delivery_minutes > 30; the second pair further filters to delivery_minutes < 60. Both criteria must be in quotes because they contain comparison symbols.

tiles.title: VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH
tiles.summary: Look up values across sheets with VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP, and INDEX/MATCH, and diagnose the three most common formula error codes.

steps.title: Finding a Driver Name from an Order Row
steps.lede: Your Orders sheet records a driver ID in column F. VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP let you pull the matching driver name from the Drivers sheet automatically.

blocks.text: Suppose your Drivers sheet has driver IDs in its leftmost column and driver names in the column next to it, and your Orders sheet records a driver ID in column F. You want each order row to show the matching driver's name without retyping it. Lookup functions do exactly that: they search one table for a key and return a value from the same row.

VLOOKUP looks up a value in the leftmost column of a range and returns a value from the same row in a column you specify by its position. Its syntax is VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup]). Entering FALSE for range_lookup searches for an exact match; leaving it blank or entering TRUE searches for an approximate match — and TRUE is the default when the argument is omitted. To look up a driver ID exactly, write =VLOOKUP(F2,Drivers!A:B,2,FALSE).

annotations.text: Lookup key column (leftmost) — VLOOKUP searches here

steps.title: HLOOKUP and XLOOKUP
steps.lede: HLOOKUP searches across rows instead of down columns. XLOOKUP is a newer alternative that works in any direction and matches exactly by default.

blocks.text: HLOOKUP works like VLOOKUP but searches across the top row of a table and returns a value from a row you specify by its position. Its syntax is HLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, row_index_num, [range_lookup]).

XLOOKUP searches lookup_array for lookup_value and returns the corresponding item from return_array, producing an exact match by default. Its syntax is XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]). VLOOKUP can only look up a value from left to right, but XLOOKUP works in any direction. The same driver lookup written as =XLOOKUP(F2,Drivers!A:A,Drivers!B:B) already matches exactly, without needing FALSE spelled out.

steps.title: HLOOKUP: Row Index
steps.lede: Test your understanding of HLOOKUP's row_index_num argument.

steps.title: Write VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP Formulas
steps.lede: Use the QuickDeliver Orders and Drivers sheets to write lookup formulas that return driver names.

steps.title: When the Key Column Is Not on the Left
steps.lede: VLOOKUP requires the lookup key to be in the leftmost column. When the layout is reversed, INDEX and MATCH work together to handle it.

blocks.text: VLOOKUP only works when the column you're returning a value from sits to the right of the key column. If your Drivers sheet instead had driver names in column A and driver IDs in column B, VLOOKUP couldn't look up an ID and return the name to its left.

MATCH searches for a specified item in a range of cells and returns the relative position of that item within the range. Its syntax is MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, [match_type]). Setting match_type to 0 finds an exact match; a match_type of 1, or omitting the argument, finds the largest value less than or equal to lookup_value and requires lookup_array to be sorted in ascending order.
INDEX returns the value of an element in a range or array, selected by its row and column position. The array form's syntax is INDEX(array, row_num, [column_num]).

annotations.text: Return column (driver_name) — sits LEFT of the key
Key column (driver_id) — VLOOKUP cannot look left from here

steps.title: Combining INDEX and MATCH
steps.lede: MATCH finds the row; INDEX retrieves the value. Together they handle any column layout.

blocks.text: VLOOKUP can only look up a value from left to right — the column containing the lookup value must be to the left of the column containing the return value. When the layout isn't built that way, MATCH can find the row position of the key and INDEX can then return the value from any column at that row position. On your Orders sheet, with a driver ID in F2, =INDEX(Drivers!A:A,MATCH(F2,Drivers!B:B,0)) finds the row where that driver ID occurs in column B of the Drivers sheet, then reads the driver name from column A at that same row — something VLOOKUP alone couldn't do on this layout.

steps.title: Reading #N/A and #REF! Error Codes
steps.lede: When a formula can't find what it needs or points to a cell that no longer exists, Excel shows an error code instead of a value.

blocks.text: Formulas in your Orders or Drivers sheets sometimes show an error code instead of a value. Each code points at a different kind of problem.

The #N/A error generally indicates that a formula can't find what it's been asked to look for. The most common cause is with XLOOKUP, VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, LOOKUP, or MATCH functions when the lookup value doesn't exist in the source data. A VLOOKUP for a driver ID that was never entered on the Drivers sheet would show #N/A.

The #REF! error shows when a formula refers to a cell that's not valid, which happens most often when cells that were referenced by formulas get deleted or pasted over. Deleting the amount column that a SUM formula depended on would turn that formula into a #REF! error.

steps.title: The #VALUE! Error and SUM vs. Arithmetic
steps.lede: A text value in a cell can break an arithmetic formula but not a SUM — knowing the difference helps you fix the right thing.

blocks.text: #VALUE! is Excel's way of saying there's something wrong with the way a formula is typed, or something wrong with the cells it's referencing. A formula like =A1+B1+C1 can break and return #VALUE! if any referenced cell contains a non-numeric (text) value, whereas a SUM formula over the same cells ignores the text values and sums only the numeric ones — so typing a stray note into an amount cell breaks a plain + formula but not a SUM over the same range.
If AVERAGE or SUM refer to cells that contain #VALUE! errors, the formulas will result in a #VALUE! error too — so one bad cell's error can spread into a SUM or AVERAGE built on top of it.

steps.title: Seeing Formula Errors Appear and Propagate
Diagnosing #VALUE! Errors
steps.lede: Identify the cause of a #VALUE! error and the fix that avoids it.

steps.title: #VALUE! Propagation Through SUM or AVERAGE
steps.lede: Understand how a single error cell can spread into formulas built on top of it.

steps.title: Diagnose Formula Errors
steps.lede: Given a worksheet with a broken VLOOKUP showing #N/A and a broken addition formula showing #VALUE!, identify the cause of each error.

steps.title: Lookups and Error Codes — Key Points
steps.lede: You can now look up values across sheets and read the three most common formula error codes.

blocks.text: VLOOKUP searches the leftmost column and returns a value by column position; use FALSE for an exact match. XLOOKUP works in any direction and matches exactly by default. When the return column sits left of the key column, combine INDEX and MATCH: MATCH finds the row position, INDEX retrieves the value. #N/A means the lookup value was not found; #REF! means a referenced cell is invalid; #VALUE! means a wrong data type — and, as covered earlier, SUM or AVERAGE over cells containing #VALUE! errors also return #VALUE!.

blocks.title: Next: Pivot Tables
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll build PivotTables that summarise your Orders data by city, status, and amount — no formulas required.

remediation_steps.title: VLOOKUP vs. HLOOKUP: Columns vs. Rows
remediation_steps.lede: A clear contrast between the two functions shows which argument controls the return position.

blocks.text: VLOOKUP searches down the leftmost column and uses col_index_num to pick which column to return — =VLOOKUP(F2,Drivers!A:B,2,FALSE) returns the value in the 2nd column. HLOOKUP searches across the top row and uses row_index_num to pick which row to return — =HLOOKUP("Delivered",A1:D3,2,FALSE) returns the value in the 2nd row. The key difference: VLOOKUP counts columns; HLOOKUP counts rows.

remediation_steps.title: INDEX and MATCH: Two Steps, One Result
remediation_steps.lede: See how MATCH produces a row number and INDEX uses it to return a value.

blocks.text: On the QuickDeliver Orders sheet, driver ID D03 is in cell F4. MATCH(F4,Drivers!B:B,0) searches column B of the Drivers sheet for D03 and returns its row position — say 4. INDEX(Drivers!A:A,4) then returns the value in row 4 of column A, which is the driver name. The full formula =INDEX(Drivers!A:A,MATCH(F4,Drivers!B:B,0)) combines both steps. VLOOKUP cannot do this because the return column (A) is to the left of the key column (B).

remediation_steps.title: #VALUE!: Text in a Number Cell
remediation_steps.lede: See the exact difference between an arithmetic formula and SUM when one cell holds text.

blocks.text: In the QuickDeliver Orders sheet, amount in row 16 holds the text "N/A" instead of a number. The formula =D2+D16 returns #VALUE! because the + operator cannot add text. The formula =SUM(D2:D21) returns a total because SUM ignores text values and sums only the numeric ones. Switching from + to SUM resolves the #VALUE! error without removing the text cell.

remediation_steps.title: #VALUE! Spreads Upward
remediation_steps.lede: One bad cell's error can propagate into any formula that references it.

blocks.text: If cell D16 already contains a #VALUE! error, then =AVERAGE(D2:D21) will also return #VALUE! — not a number — because AVERAGE and SUM propagate errors from cells they reference. The error in D16 spreads into any formula built on top of it. Fixing D16 (for example, by replacing the text with a valid number) clears the error from all dependent formulas at once.

tiles.title: Removing Duplicates and Splitting Text
tiles.summary: Clean your Orders data by removing duplicate rows, split combined text into separate columns, and write formulas that reference cells on other sheets.

steps.title: Removing Duplicate Rows Permanently
steps.lede: When the same order number appears twice in your Orders sheet, Excel's Remove Duplicates tool clears the extras — but the deletion is permanent.

blocks.text: Say the same order number shows up twice in your Orders sheet — maybe it was entered once by mistake. Excel has a dedicated tool for this, but it's worth being careful with.
When you use the Remove Duplicates feature, the duplicate data is permanently deleted, so it's a good idea to copy the original data to another worksheet before removing duplicates.

To remove duplicates, select the range of cells that has duplicate values, select Data > Remove Duplicates, and then check or uncheck the columns under Columns to choose which columns are used to identify a duplicate row. On your Orders sheet, checking only the order_id column means two rows with the same order number get treated as duplicates even if other columns differ — while checking every column would only catch rows that match everywhere.

steps.title: Splitting One Column into Two
steps.lede: When a single cell holds combined text like "Lagos,Nigeria", Text to Columns splits it into separate columns using a delimiter you choose.

blocks.text: To split text into columns, select the cell or column that contains the text, select Data > Text to Columns, choose Delimited, select the delimiter(s) such as Comma or Space, choose the destination for the split data, and select Finish. If your Orders sheet has a single column holding "Lagos,Nigeria" as one text value, running Text to Columns with Comma as the delimiter splits it into two columns.

steps.title: Referencing Cells on Another Sheet
steps.lede: A formula on your Orders sheet can pull a value directly from your Drivers sheet — or even from a different workbook — using a cross-sheet reference.

blocks.text: A formula can refer to a cell on another sheet in the same workbook by writing the sheet name followed by an exclamation point (!) and then the cell or range reference, for example Marketing!B1. So a formula on your Orders sheet that needs a value sitting on your Drivers sheet could reference Drivers!B1.

If the referenced worksheet's name contains spaces or numbers, the name must be enclosed in single quotation marks in the reference, for example ='January Revenue'!A1. So if you renamed your drivers tab to "Driver List", a reference to it would need to be written 'Driver List'!A1, not Driver List!A1.

A workbook link to a cell range in another workbook, when the source workbook is open, includes the workbook name in square brackets, followed by the worksheet name, an exclamation point, and the cells the formula depends on, for example =SUM([Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10:C25).

Bottom example: 'January Revenue'!A1 with a callout on the single quotes around the sheet name that contains a space. A third example shows [Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10:C25 with the workbook name in square brackets labelled.

steps.title: Cleaning, Splitting, and Linking — Key Points
steps.lede: You can now remove duplicate rows safely, split delimited text into columns, and reference cells across sheets.

blocks.text: Remove Duplicates permanently deletes matched rows — copy your data first. Choose which columns define a duplicate: checking only order_id catches same-ID rows even if other columns differ. Text to Columns splits a delimited column in three steps: choose Delimited, pick the delimiter (Comma, Space, or other), then Finish. Cross-sheet references use the syntax SheetName!CellAddress; if the sheet name contains spaces or numbers, wrap it in single quotes: 'Sheet Name'!A1. Cross-workbook links add the workbook name in square brackets: [Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10.

blocks.title: Next: Formula Syntax and References
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll write formulas with arithmetic operators, understand operator precedence, and lock cells with absolute references using the $ sign.

remediation_steps.title: Why Copy Before Removing Duplicates
remediation_steps.lede: See the contrast between a reversible and an irreversible operation.

blocks.text: Sorting your Orders sheet is reversible — you can sort again in a different order. Remove Duplicates is not: once you click OK, the matched rows are gone and there is no undo after you save. Copying the sheet to a backup tab first means you can always recover the original rows if you removed too many. The copy step takes seconds; recovering without it can be impossible.

remediation_steps.title: Text to Columns: The Three Steps
remediation_steps.lede: Walk through the wizard steps one more time with a concrete example.

blocks.text: Starting from a column that holds "Lagos,Nigeria" in each cell: (1) select the column, (2) click Data > Text to Columns, (3) choose Delimited and click Next, (4) check Comma as the delimiter — the preview shows the split — (5) choose a destination cell and click Finish. The single column becomes two: one with "Lagos" and one with "Nigeria". Choosing Space instead of Comma would split on the space character instead.

remediation_steps.title: Cross-Sheet vs. Cross-Workbook Syntax
remediation_steps.lede: Compare the two reference forms side by side.

blocks.text: Same workbook, simple sheet name: Drivers!B1 — sheet name, exclamation point, cell address. Same workbook, sheet name with a space: 'January Revenue'!A1 — single quotes wrap the name. Different workbook (source open): =SUM([Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10:C25) — workbook name in square brackets before the sheet name. The square brackets only appear for cross-workbook links; within the same workbook you never use them.

remediation_steps.title: When Do Sheet Names Need Quotes?
remediation_steps.lede: The quoting rule is simple: any name that contains a space or a number needs single quotes.

blocks.text: Drivers!B1 — no quotes needed; the name has no spaces or numbers. 'January Revenue'!A1 — quotes required; the name contains a space. '2024 Orders'!C5 — quotes required; the name contains a number. Forgetting the quotes when they're needed causes a formula error. A safe habit: always click the sheet tab while typing the formula and let Excel insert the correct syntax automatically.

tiles.title: Sorting and Filtering Data
tiles.summary: Reorder your Orders sheet by one or more columns, and use AutoFilter to show only the rows that meet your criteria.

steps.title: Putting Your Orders in Order
steps.lede: Sorting rearranges your Orders sheet rows by the values in one or more columns — oldest first, largest first, or any combination.

blocks.text: With a week of orders in your Orders sheet, you often want them in a particular order rather than the order they were entered in — oldest first, or largest amount first.

To sort a column of numbers, select a cell in that column and, on the Data tab in the Sort & Filter group, select Sort Smallest to Largest or Sort Largest to Smallest. To sort a column of dates or times, select a cell in that column and select Sort Oldest to Newest or Sort Newest to Oldest instead.

To sort by more than one column, open the Sort dialog from Data > Sort, choose the first column in the Sort by box, then select Add Level to add another column. Entries higher in the list are sorted before entries lower in the list. Each level has its own Order setting, so different columns within the same multi-level sort can be sorted in different directions.

blocks.alt_text: Excel Sort dialog with two levels configured. Level 1 shows Sort by: order_date, Order: Oldest to Newest. Level 2 shows Then by: amount, Order: Largest to Smallest. Each level has its own independent Order dropdown.

steps.title: Showing Only the Rows You Need
steps.lede: AutoFilter hides rows that don't match your criteria — the data is still there, just not visible. Clearing the filter brings it all back.

blocks.text: Sometimes you don't want to reorder your Orders sheet, you want to see only some of it — for example, only the orders above a certain amount.

To filter a range of data, select any cell within the range, select Data > Filter, select the column header's filter arrow, choose Number Filters or Text Filters and a comparison such as Greater Than, enter the filter criteria, and select OK. AutoFilter shows the data you want and hides the rest; clearing a filter redisplays all of the data.

A range or table can be filtered by more than one column at once; filters are additive, so each additional filter further reduces the subset of data shown. Filtering your Orders sheet to amounts greater than 5000, then filtering the city column to Lagos, leaves only the Lagos orders above 5000 — both conditions apply together, not separately.

steps.title: Sorting and Filtering — Key Points
steps.lede: You can now sort by one or more columns with independent directions, and filter to show only the rows that match your criteria.

blocks.text: To sort numbers, use Sort Smallest to Largest or Largest to Smallest from the Data tab. To sort dates, use Sort Oldest to Newest or Newest to Oldest. For multi-level sorts, open Data > Sort, add levels with Add Level, and set each level's Order independently — higher levels are applied first. AutoFilter hides rows that don't match; clearing the filter redisplays all data. Filters are additive: each additional column filter further reduces the visible subset.

remediation_steps.title: Multi-Level Sort: Each Level Has Its Own Direction
remediation_steps.lede: See the contrast between a single-level sort and a two-level sort with different directions.

blocks.text: Single-level sort: sort the Orders sheet by amount Largest to Smallest — all rows reorder by amount alone. Two-level sort: Level 1 is order_date Oldest to Newest; Level 2 is amount Largest to Smallest. The result: rows are grouped by date in ascending order, and within each date the rows are ordered by amount descending. The key point is that Level 2's direction (Largest to Smallest) is completely independent of Level 1's direction (Oldest to Newest) — you set each in its own Order dropdown.

remediation_steps.title: AutoFilter: Hide vs. Delete
remediation_steps.lede: Filtering hides rows — it never removes them. Clearing the filter brings them back.

blocks.text: After applying a Number Filter (Greater Than 5000) to the amount column of your Orders sheet, rows with amounts of 5000 or less disappear from view — but they are still in the sheet. The row numbers jump (e.g. 1, 3, 7 …) because the hidden rows are still there. Clicking Data > Filter again, or clicking Clear in the Sort & Filter group, removes the filter and all rows reappear. No data was deleted.

tiles.title: Structured Tables and Named Ranges
tiles.summary: Convert a data range into an Excel table with structured references, and name ranges for readable formulas.

steps.title: From Plain Range to Structured Table
steps.lede: Converting your Orders range into a table gives every column a label and lets formulas refer to columns by name.

blocks.text: Your Orders sheet keeps growing as new deliveries come in. Converting its range into an Excel table gives each column a labeled header, lets formulas refer to columns by name, and lets the table expand automatically as you add data just below or beside it.

To create a table from a data range, select the cell or range, then choose Home > Format as Table and pick a table style. By default the resulting table has a header row that labels each column, though that header row can be turned off if it isn't wanted.

Once a range is a table, formulas can refer to its columns by name instead of by raw cell address — this is called a structured reference. Instead of =SUM(C2:C7), a formula can use =SUM(DeptSales[Sales Amount]), naming the table and the column directly. On an Orders table that same pattern looks like =SUM(Orders[Amount]).

blocks.text: The table also grows with your data on its own: typing a value in a cell just below the table's last row, or in a cell to the right of its last column, expands the table to include that new row or column. As tomorrow's deliveries are typed in just below your existing Orders table, the table expands to include those new rows.

blocks.text: A named range lets a formula use a readable label instead of a raw cell address. To name a cell or range, select it, type a name into the Name Box, and press Enter — for example, selecting C2:C51 (the delivery-time column) and naming it DeliveryTimes.

Once a name is defined, typing the name into a formula — or selecting Formulas > Use in Formula and choosing the name — lets that formula reference the named range instead of its raw address. A formula can refer to DeliveryTimes instead of C2:C51.

tiles.title: Pivot Tables
tiles.summary: Build a PivotTable to summarise Orders data by city and status, then change the value-field summary function.

steps.title: What a PivotTable Does and How to Build One
steps.lede: A PivotTable summarises your Orders data by city, status, or any other field — no formulas required.

blocks.text: Reading down a long Orders sheet to compare total amounts by city and status by hand would take forever. A PivotTable is a tool to calculate, summarize, and analyze data that lets you see comparisons, patterns, and trends in your data.

To create a PivotTable, select the data cells, select Insert > PivotTable, choose where to place the PivotTable report, and select OK. To add a field, select its checkbox in the PivotTable Fields pane; non-numeric fields go to Rows and numeric fields go to Values by default. A field can be moved to a different area by dragging it there.

Filters area fields appear as top-level report filters above the PivotTable. Columns area fields appear as Column Labels at the top. Rows area fields appear as Row Labels on the left. Values area fields appear as summarised numeric values in the body. Building a PivotTable from your Orders data with City in Rows, Status in Columns, and Amount in Values gives a grid of summarised order amounts for every city/status combination.

steps.title: Changing How Values Are Summarised
steps.lede: The Values area defaults to Sum for numbers and Count for text — and you can change it.

blocks.text: Data in a PivotTable's Values area summarises the underlying source data by default using the SUM function for numeric values and the COUNT function for text values. Placing Amount in Values on your Orders PivotTable defaults to a total of every matching order's amount, not an average.

To change a value field's summary function, select the field in the Values area, then on the PivotTable Analyze tab select Active Field > Field Settings (or right-click the value and choose Value Field Settings), select the Summarize Values By tab, and choose the function you want, such as Average. Switching Amount from Sum to Average turns the same PivotTable from showing total revenue per city into showing average order value per city.

blocks.text: To create a PivotTable: select the data cells, choose Insert > PivotTable, pick where to place the report, and click OK. In the Fields pane, check City — it goes to Rows because it is text. Check Amount — it goes to Values because it is numeric. Drag Status to Columns. The result: Row Labels show cities on the left, Column Labels show statuses at the top, and the body shows summarised amounts. Filters area fields would appear above the table as top-level report filters.

remediation_steps.title: Choosing Fields and Areas for a Summarisation Task
remediation_steps.lede: Match the question you want to answer to the correct field placement.

blocks.text: To answer 'What is the total order amount per city?' place City in Rows and Amount in Values — the PivotTable sums Amount for each city. To add a breakdown by status, drag Status to Columns. To filter to a single city, drag City to Filters instead of Rows. Non-numeric fields added to the Fields pane go to Rows by default; numeric fields go to Values. You can always drag a field from one area to another.

remediation_steps.title: Sum vs. Count: The Default Rule
remediation_steps.lede: The data type of the field determines which summary function the PivotTable uses by default.

blocks.text: When you drag a numeric field such as Amount into the Values area, the PivotTable defaults to Sum — it adds up all matching values. When you drag a text field such as Status into Values, the PivotTable defaults to Count — it counts how many rows match. You can always change the function via Value Field Settings.

tiles.title: Chart Types
tiles.summary: Build bar, line, and pie charts from Orders data to visualise comparisons, trends, and part-of-whole shares.

steps.title: Bar Charts: Comparing Categories
steps.lede: A bar chart places categories on one axis and values on the other to show comparisons at a glance.

blocks.text: Bar charts illustrate comparisons among individual items; in a bar chart, the categories are typically organised along one axis and the values along the other. A summary table of total order amount by city is exactly the kind of category-versus-value data a bar chart compares.

To create a chart, select the data, choose Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it. If you don't see a bar chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and click OK.

blocks.caption: City order totals — source data for a bar chart. Each city is a category; total_amount is the value.

steps.title: Line Charts: Showing Trends Over Time
steps.lede: A line chart distributes evenly-spaced time intervals along the horizontal axis and values along the vertical axis.

blocks.text: In a line chart, category data is distributed evenly along the horizontal axis and value data along the vertical axis. Line charts can show continuous data over time on an evenly scaled axis, making them well suited to showing trends at equal intervals such as months, quarters, or fiscal years. A summary of total order amount by month is exactly this kind of evenly-spaced, time-ordered data.

To create a line chart, select the data, choose Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it. If you don't see a line chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and click OK.

steps.title: Pie Charts: Part-of-Whole Shares
steps.lede: A pie chart shows each category's share of a total — but only when the data meets four conditions.

blocks.text: Pie charts show the size of items in one data series proportional to the sum of the items. They are appropriate when you have only one data series to plot, none of the values are negative, there are no more than seven categories, and the categories represent parts of the whole pie. A summary of total order amount by city, for no more than seven cities, fits that description as long as no amount is negative.

To create a pie chart, select the data, choose Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it. If you don't see a pie chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and click OK.

steps.title: Chart Types — Key Points
steps.lede: You can now build bar, line, and pie charts and choose the right type for your data.

blocks.text: Bar charts compare categories: the category axis holds labels and the value axis holds bar heights. Line charts show trends over equal time intervals: months, quarters, or fiscal years go on the horizontal axis and values on the vertical axis. Pie charts show part-of-whole shares and require one data series, no negative values, no more than seven categories, and categories that sum to a meaningful whole. For all three types, select the data and use Insert > Recommended Charts to preview and insert.

blocks.title: Next: Python Figures and Layouts
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll move from spreadsheet charts to Python's matplotlib, building figures with axes and controlling layout programmatically.

remediation_steps.title: Bar Chart Axis Encoding and Creation Steps
remediation_steps.lede: A clear contrast shows which data goes on which axis and how to insert the chart.

blocks.text: In a bar chart, categories go on one axis and values on the other. For the city totals table, city names go on the category axis and total_amount values determine bar height. To insert: select the city and total_amount columns, choose Insert > Recommended Charts, preview the bar chart, and click OK. If the bar chart is not on the Recommended tab, open All Charts, select Bar, and click OK.

remediation_steps.title: Line Chart Axis Roles and When to Use One
remediation_steps.lede: Equal time intervals on the horizontal axis make a line chart the right choice.

blocks.text: In a line chart, category data — typically time labels such as Jan-2024, Feb-2024 — is distributed evenly along the horizontal axis, and value data goes on the vertical axis. Line charts are well suited to data measured at equal intervals: months, quarters, or fiscal years. The monthly summary table has six months at equal intervals, so a line chart shows the trend clearly. A table of city totals is not time-ordered, so a bar chart is more appropriate there.

remediation_steps.title: Pie Chart Eligibility and Creation
remediation_steps.lede: Four conditions must hold before a pie chart is appropriate.

blocks.text: A pie chart is appropriate when: (1) you have only one data series to plot, (2) none of the values are negative, (3) there are no more than seven categories, and (4) the categories represent parts of the whole. The city totals table has six cities (≤ 7), all positive amounts, one series, and the cities together represent all orders — so a pie chart is appropriate. To insert: select the city and total_amount columns, choose Insert > Recommended Charts, preview the pie chart, and click OK.

tiles.title: Conditional Formatting and Data Validation
tiles.summary: Apply automatic cell formatting based on value rules, and restrict what users can enter into a cell.

steps.title: Highlighting Cells Automatically by Value
steps.lede: Conditional formatting applies a format to cells based on rules you create — no manual colouring needed.

blocks.text: Conditional formatting applies a format to cells automatically based on rules you create that determine the format based on the cells' values — rather than you manually colouring cells one at a time.

To apply a quick conditional formatting rule, select the cells, then on the Home tab in the Style group select Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules, choose a comparison command such as Less Than, enter the comparison value, and select a format. Selecting the delivery-time column and applying Highlight Cells Rules > Less Than with a value of 15 and a green fill automatically colours every delivery under 15 minutes.

steps.title: Restricting What Users Can Enter
steps.lede: Data validation restricts the type of data or values users can enter into a cell, and can display a custom error message.

blocks.text: Data validation restricts the type of data or the values users can enter into a cell, such as a dropdown list, and can display a customised error message when a user enters invalid data.

To add a dropdown-list validation rule, select the cells, choose Data > Data Validation, on the Settings tab set Allow to List, then in the Source box type the list values separated by commas, making sure the In-cell dropdown check box is selected. Restricting the Orders sheet's status column with Source set to Pending,Delivered,Cancelled gives each cell a dropdown of those three words.

steps.title: Numeric, Date, and Text-Length Validation
steps.lede: Data validation can also restrict entry to a number, date, or text of a specific length.

blocks.text: Data validation can restrict entry to a whole number, decimal, date, time, or text length within limits: under Allow choose the type (for example Whole Number), under Data choose a condition (for example between), and then enter the minimum, maximum, or specific value to allow. On the delivery-time column, choosing Whole Number, between 0 and 300, blocks anyone from typing a negative or unreasonably large delivery time.

steps.title: Conditional Formatting and Data Validation — Key Points
steps.lede: You can now apply automatic cell formatting rules and restrict what users can enter.

blocks.text: Conditional formatting applies a format to cells automatically based on rules you create from cell values. Use Home > Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules, choose a comparison such as Less Than, enter the threshold, and pick a format. Data validation restricts what users can enter: choose Data > Data Validation, set Allow to List and type comma-separated values for a dropdown, or choose Whole Number, Date, or Text Length with a condition and limits for numeric restrictions. A customised error message can be shown when invalid data is entered.

remediation_steps.title: Setting Up a Highlight Cells Rule
remediation_steps.lede: Walk through the exact menu path and see the rule trigger automatically.

blocks.text: Conditional formatting applies a format automatically based on cell values — you do not colour cells manually. To apply a Less Than rule to the delivery-time column: select the column cells, go to Home > Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules > Less Than, type 15 in the value box, choose a red fill, and click OK. Every cell whose value is below 15 is immediately coloured red; cells at or above 15 remain unformatted. The rule re-evaluates whenever a cell value changes.

remediation_steps.title: What Data Validation Does and How to Set Numeric Limits
remediation_steps.lede: Data validation blocks invalid input before it reaches the cell.

blocks.text: Data validation restricts the type of data or the values users can enter into a cell, and can display a customised error message when a user enters invalid data. For a numeric restriction on the delivery-time column: select the column, choose Data > Data Validation, set Allow to Whole Number, set Data to between, enter 0 as the minimum and 300 as the maximum, and click OK. Typing a negative number or a value above 300 triggers the restriction notice.

remediation_steps.title: Choosing the Right Validation Type
remediation_steps.lede: Match the input restriction requirement to the correct Allow setting.

blocks.text: Use List when you want to restrict entry to a fixed set of text values — for example, Pending, Delivered, Cancelled in the status column. Use Whole Number or Decimal when you want to restrict entry to a number within a range — for example, delivery times between 0 and 300. Use Date or Time for date or time restrictions. Use Text Length when you want to restrict how many characters can be entered. All types are set through Data > Data Validation > Settings > Allow.
